items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: And that’s how the idea of Gil Evans’ arrangements came about. And the title of the album, I told Miles and Gil is going to be “Miles Ahead,”

ctx.x: In your career as a producer, did you have a philosophy about when you approached a new artist you hadn’t worked with before about how to produce them?

Yes. The basic idea was very, very simple. How can I help the artist present himself in the most effective way for his benefit as well as of course the company? But in many cases there was a matter of what do you do to make the artist appealing to the potential record customer, and most of the time the artist had no idea except that man I just want to blow you know. And that’s why it became important as everything grew more and more competitive to find ways of presenting artists, including jazz artists, in a way…

what happened. Miles was fortunate enough to get the original quintet together very quickly in September ‘55. I went to hear them for the first time in Philadelphia when he called and said, “Hey, I’ve got these terrific guys: Coltrane— and Coltrane was just a name to me, I’d never even heard him — Philly Joe Jones and Paul Chambers and Red Garland, well I knew them of course. And he did hold them together and Wittemore did do a terrific job of booking them when there were no Columbia records to back them up so…
